maya_ng: Heads-up — ran into a weird eviction edge on a private env. Two sidecars got kicked and the runtime chose the older model version to keep alive. Why would we prefer older in tie situations?

alex_kim: oof. Was that the deterministic-tiebreaker we added last year? It falls back to lowest eviction_score and then lexicographic agent id IIRC.

sara: Wait lexicographic id? That sounds non-deterministic across deployments (different hostname schemes). Can we even rely on that for cross-env parity (hosted vs private)?

ivan: Right — design was: eviction_score = (oom_risk * 1000) + age_rank. If equal, we used instance_id ordering to avoid flakes. That was a pragmatic choice but not principled.

maya_ng: The problem is it kept the older model while the new one had proper pinned weights for the customer's private commit. Result: wrong semantics. Customer noticed.

alex_kim: Yikes. For hosted we have a central controller that can enforce model-version preference, but for private the control plane is customer-managed so our tie rules need to be conservative.

ivan: Proposal: tighten tie-breaker priority list to: 1) explicit customer pin (if present) 2) model-version compatibility score (binary compatible > legacy) 3) remaining request queue length 4) eviction_score 5) deterministic hash(seed = cluster_uuid + agent_id). That moves away from arbitrary lexicographic ordering.

sara: I like the pin first. We should also record a structured telemetry event when tie-breaker chosen: {reason, kept_agent, evicted_agent, env}. That helps audits.

alex_kim: Agreed on telemetry. Also need a fallback when private controlplane cannot assert pins — maybe the runtime should consult a locally cached pin manifest and fall back to version compatibility check.

maya_ng: And how do we define "version compatibility score"? Semantic major/minor? I think we should use model manifest capabilities: generation API compatibility, kvcache layout version, and tokenizer fingerprint. Each match adds points.

ivan: Exactly. Make it rule-based and cheaply computable. We can implement a small compatibility function in the runtime library used by all hosting modes. That keeps parity.

sara: Ops question: when we evict, do we gracefully migrate the KV cache to the kept agent or just drop it? Moving cache is expensive but avoids cold start regressions.

alex_kim: For now: if compatibility_score >= threshold AND cache_size < copy_limit, attempt async KV copy with circuit breaker. Else force drop and emit coldstart alert.

maya_ng: Sounds fair. Could we also add a "pin-precedence" config per customer for Private deployments so customers can choose strict vs best-effort? Some customers will accept downtime vs correctness tradeoffs.

ivan: Yes — add pin_mode: [strict, advisory]. Strict = block eviction that would remove pinned agent unless manual override. Advisory = used only in tiebreaks. Default = advisory for hosted.

alex_kim: Implementation notes: small runtime change + config flag + telemetry. Need a short RFC doc and an ops playbook for private installs. I can take RFC draft.

maya_ng: Awesome — please include migration steps and a recovery command to rebind KV caches (if copy fails). Also add unit tests for deterministic-hash behavior across cluster_uuid permutations.

deploy-bot: deploy queued: "eviction-tiebreaker-v2" to staging at 2025-11-17T16:02:00Z :rocket:

maya_ng: thanks — will validate with the customer tomorrow.
